newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French steelmaker Usinor's '96 profits slide.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French steelmaker Usinor's '96 profits slide.

text.p: French steelmaking giant Usinor Sacilor, privatised last year, reported on Tuesday that 1996 profits tumbled, hit by lower demand and weaker prices, and it cut its full-year dividend.
But the company managed to slash its debt by nearly half to 6.5 billion francs ($1.1 billion) from 11.0 billion francs.
Usinor Sacilor chairman Francis Mer said he hoped that the steelmaker would improve earnings in 1997, helped by a rebound in demand.

"There should be a significant upturn in the second half of 1997 regarding earnings," he told a news conference, saying the first half of the year was looking disappointing. "We're hoping to do better in 1997."
The steelmaker said net attributable profit in 1996 slid to 1.49 billion francs from a record 4.43 billion on turnover that fell to 71.06 billion francs from 78.42 billion.
On a like-for-like basis, turnover was down 8.6 percent, due to lower volumes and price falls.
Usinor cut its dividend to three francs per share from four francs but that reduction was smaller than some financial analysts had feared.
Operating profit slumped to 2.5 billion francs from 8.0 billion francs, despite better financial results due to to lower debt and dividends from unconsolidated interests.

Sales were driven by flat carbon steels totalling 35.10 billion francs, down 7.6 percent. Sales of stainless steels and alloys were 16.5 percent lower at 16.33 billion francs while turnover in specialty steels fell nine percent to 13.60 billion francs.

Some 33.6 percent of sales were in France, 43.1 percent in other European countries and 23.3 percent in the rest of the world. The United States accounted for 11.8 percent of total sales. The geographic breakdown of sales was similar to 1995.
The company said demand was starting to rebound significantly in stainless and flat carbon products in Europe.
"Although price charges are still low for the first quarter, some improvement can be seen, specifically in galvanized products," it said.
But the company warned that while volumes were up, "average prices, at least for the first half, should be lower than those of 1996".
Industrial investments rose to 3.94 billion francs from 3.02 billion.
